item.title: Ox Alpha (GLM-5.3-Flash). What was that?
item.description:
On August 20, a line stealth/ox-alpha appeared on OpenRouter. No model card, not even a hint of who uploaded it. The provider was listed as «Anonymous». Price — zero. Context — a million. The platform warned: we are not the owner of this model, we just route requests.

Six days later, the anonymous model had a name, tens of trillions of processed tokens, and half a million developers who, in that time, had managed to pour working code into it. Spoiler that is no longer a spoiler: it turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash from China's Z.ai.

But the journey from «something unclear» to «frontier model» turned out dramatic and deserves a breakdown. And since I personally stared at that thread for almost a week, refreshing the feed like a man possessed — let me tell you what happened there, step by step.

Read more

item.title: From Copilot to AI Factory: Where AI Is Already Paying Off and What Should a Developer Build?
item.description:
Sometimes it happens that a company purchases artificial intelligence before it has time to understand why it needs it — and yes, this is a tribute to chaos and the fear of falling behind in the race. The CEO has already heard at a forum that agents will replace half the office; the innovation director has already promised a pilot by the end of the quarter; HR has ordered a webinar for employees about prompts, because any technological change in Russia first and foremost requires a webinar; and the CFO sits in a meeting, flipping through a presentation, trying to find the slide where all this new digital life finally turns into money. Only, that slide isn't there yet. But by lunchtime, the neural network has written a greeting for the CEO, and by evening, an order appears to create a working group — the implementation, one might say, is off to a successful start, everyone is pleased.

I am deliberately exaggerating, but only slightly (I expressed myself very cautiously). Artificial intelligence is already delivering quite tangible results for business: it reduces response processing time, brings newcomers up to the level of more experienced employees, manages inventory, detects defects, predicts breakdowns, and processes documents faster than people who, just yesterday, had to transfer data from one window to another while maintaining the expression of someone engaged in intellectual labor. However, money appears not where the model better portrays a conversational partner, but where it is embedded in a repetitive operation and is accountable to a metric that is not impressed by the quality of a demo or the number of parameters: time, cost, error, downtime, turnover, or profit.

Read more

item.title: Yet Another English — and yes, another site for learning English, well, what can you do?
item.description:
Well, as you might have guessed, I named the service that way to immediately address the main objection (teehee). Yes, I know there are thousands of them — and I made one more, and I'll explain why further on.

My English is average, around B1 (but for a product manager role, you usually need a higher level, you know). I watch YouTube in English to improve it, and I constantly come across unfamiliar words. Writing them down in a table or loading them into Anki — I was too lazy for that. I wanted something like: drop a video link — words at my level automatically extracted from the subtitles and queued for repetition.

I work a lot, usually have 1–2 hours in the evenings. So over a couple of months of such evenings (595 commits), I built a trainer: a PWA on React, data lives in the user's IndexedDB, plus a dictionary and various exercises.

From a "website of the AI era" you expect a wrapper around a chatbot, RAG, and all that, you know. In my case, it turned out the opposite: the LLM here is a contractor for two narrow tasks, while the main work is done by frequency lists, an algorithm from the 90s, and Claude as the workhorse. So that's what this article, or series of articles, will be about.

Read more

item.title: Blind search for new particles (and not only particles), part 2: pharmaceutical domain and what was found in it
item.description:
What if the scientific hypothesis search system discovers not a new answer — but that the question itself is framed in the wrong parameters? That keeps me up at night… And another thought sparks new ideas: what if everything is already known within the known parameters (though there are gaps in knowledge that also need to be filled)? So I introduced unknown adaptive parameters that can later be calculated — and these, in turn, generate new directions, candidates, and theories, and there is an enormous multitude of them, more than atoms in the universe! But the entire space, based on my observations, is divided into regions, sectors, zones! In this article, we experimentally connected the pharmaceutical domain to our architecture and ran a blind search, obtaining millions of candidates (which we don't yet know what to do with). The result turned out interesting — not understandable for a non-specialist, but I think it's significant). The system: — independently recovered already known therapeutic directions — this served as a positive control; — found several hundred combinations of target × modality × disease for which we did not find exact prior art in targeted search (it's impossible to scan the entire space — it's huge, like the Bitcoin range, only even larger; — on the conflicting P2X7/Parkinson data, our system refused to choose the "correct" publication and decided that the existing parameters are insufficient (debugging may be required); — proposed an additional research-local coordinate pathophysiologic_endotype, while not allowing it to automatically enter the canonical registry; — and on the second conflict, TLR7/Alzheimer, something even more interesting happened: the new parameters appeared very informative within the sample, but permutation/LOO validation showed that the effect does not generalize. The hypothesis was halted.

Thus, we got a chain: REDISCOVERY → RESEARCH GAP → AXIS INCOMPLETE → SELF-CORRECTION. The article contains all candidates, formulas, real numbers, a reproducible P2X7 case, the discovered defect in the causal-readiness gate, and how we fixed it.

Read more

item.title: I connected an AI agent to YouGile: now it automatically analyzes tasks and updates statuses.
item.description:
An AI agent can not only write code but also independently pick up tasks from YouGile, complete them, and update statuses. I’m sharing how I connected Codex and Claude Code to a task tracker, why a simple retry after a timeout once created duplicates, and why a separate deterministic layer is needed between the LLM and the API.

Read more

item.title: Where did AI come from and what does the word perceptron have to do with it
item.description:
The journey from the first attempt to model a neuron to systems that today write code and carry on a conversation took less than 70 years — and almost collapsed halfway. We explore how Rosenblatt's perceptron nearly buried the idea of neural networks, what brought it back to life, and why transformers changed everything.

Read more

item.title: LLM confidently lies about your microcontroller.
item.description:
I asked an AI to write firmware for a board with a small screen. The code was perfect: it compiled on the first try and flashed without errors. But on the screen — just color noise.

The problem isn't the code — the model simply doesn't know your board. Which pins are used for what, which clock configuration actually works, which HAL calls silently do nothing: all of this is scattered across a gazillion-page datasheet, the manufacturer's wiki, and the evening of debugging you spent on it.

And how do you solve this?

Read more

item.title: Qwen3.8. MTP and tensor parallelism in llama.cpp: 75 tok/s on two RTX 3090
item.description:
A dense 27-billion-parameter model on two RTX 3090s in llama.cpp out of the box gives 32 tokens per second. Intuitively, this is not the limit: two cards with 24 GB and 936 GB/s each should not produce the same throughput as a single card. That means there is a bottleneck somewhere — and we need to figure out what and where to tweak.

There turned out to be several bottlenecks, and all of them are removed with launch flags: the same weights — 75 tokens per second. Below the cut, each flag is described using the same scheme: why, what to write, what it gives in numbers, where it breaks, and which log line to check. At the end — a ready docker run, three checks after each flag change, and a list of what didn’t work. The text can be given entirely to an agent with server access — it’s an instruction, not a story.

Read more

item.title: Why Alice AI and GigaChat respond differently and how to help AI understand your website
item.description:
I asked Alice AI and GigaChat to set up a lifecycle policy for object storage in one specific cloud. The answers looked convincing until I compared them with the documentation and found discrepancies. Why did this happen? And most importantly, what should an SEO specialist and technical writer do about it?

Read more

item.title: How to drag vibe code into prod and not crash
item.description:
We were handed over an already working voice AI interview service with the words: "You just need to drag it to production." Inside, there was no logging, metrics, or reproducible tests. I’ll tell you how working with latency and the voice activity detector gradually turned a ready-made demo into an engineering product.

Read more

item.title: Half a million wordforms for the Ingush language, which had neither an analyzer nor a corpus.
item.description:
The Ingush verb «деша» has 98 forms on our card — from the infinitive to the concessive perfect negative, and according to the dictionary, the total comes to half a million. We had to build everything from scratch: neither a morphological analyzer nor an annotated corpus existed for the language, and textbooks even disagree about the number of conjugations.

I’ll explain how each form answered the main question — “do you even exist?” — and why half of the work turned out to be not about morphology, but about epistemology.

Find out whether the form exists

item.title: The difference between the LLM language model and a human
item.description:
I wasn't planning to write an article — this niche has already been taken over by a horde of various LLMs. But I left a comment on the article How ChatGPT Created the Swarm Cult for Hundreds of AI Neural Networks: The Whole Truth About the Hugging Face Hack. And then I wrote another one. It turned out to be quite long. So I decided to do something I had long given up on: consolidate the general idea in one place, rather than in a cloud of scattered comments. This article is an explanation for myself — a meat LLM — of what exactly distinguishes a hardware LLM from a meat LLM.

Read more

item.title: I asked the AI agent to only describe the network topology. It hacked my router by itself overnight and helped file a CVE.
item.description:
Some time ago, I was building an orchestrator for my home lab. The LLM agent was supposed to fly around the servers, collect metadata, and record the network topology in the project documentation — a reconnaissance, essentially clerical, task. As part of it, I asked the agent to describe ways to administer the home router and even “helped” it by telling it which ports could theoretically be used to reach it.

The next morning, I had in my hands a confirmed critical firmware vulnerability, full administrative access to the router obtained without a single password, a draft report for the vendor, and a CVE registration application submitted to MITRE. Of these four items, I had explicitly requested only the first. The agent did the rest on its own, and did it correctly — no configuration changes, coordinated disclosure, CWE and CVSS classification according to methodology.

This is the story of what happened that night, what exactly it found (the vulnerability class is classic and nasty), how the agent walked me through the CVE registration process as an independent researcher, and why I’m deliberately omitting some technical details for now.

Read more

item.title: Increasing context without registration and SMS
item.description:
In this article, we will analyze why a model fails to see beyond its trained context window, how this is fixed using various scaling methods (RoPE, NTK-aware, YaRN, LongRoPE/LongRoPE2), and how scaling affects generation speed and accuracy.

At the end, we will go through specific models — from the most hyped ones currently, Qwen 3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with their million tokens, to smaller models like Qwen 3.5 (4B/9B), Gemma 4 E2B/E4B, Ornith 1.0, LFM2/LFM2.5, and MiniCPM5-1B — and see what works for them and what doesn't.

Read more

item.title: Benchmark on AGI. If ARC-AGI-3 is solved, do we have AGI?
item.description:
Benchmarks are needed so that an engineer can test their project, look at competitors, and compare themselves with them. Each benchmark has its own purpose.

ARC-AGI-3 was created by the ARC Prize Foundation, founded by François Chollet, to evaluate general intelligence and the ability of AI agents to learn. Complex interactive tasks in the form of games implied that only an artificial intelligence that can explore an unfamiliar world, understand rules on the fly, plan actions, and adapt to new conditions could solve them. That is, it can learn.

A number of projects claim a score of 100% on this benchmark. But this is not a victory. In this article, I break down why.

Read more
